1.title: Governance Concepts: Laws, Frameworks, Policies, Standards and Procedures
1.text: Welcome to Module three: Governance Concepts: Laws, Frameworks, Policies, Standards and Procedures. It covers the exam area one. Security Principles. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. one point three Understand governance concepts: Regulations and laws. Frameworks and guidelines. Policies, standards (for example I S O, Center for Internet Security), procedures. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: one. Security Principles (twenty-four percent). Exam format: an adaptive exam of one hundred to one hundred twenty-five questions in two hours; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official I S C two C C exam outline.

1.title: Governance in one sentence
1.text: Governance in one sentence. Governance is how the leaders of an organization direct and oversee security so that it supports the business and meets its duties. Management then carries out that direction. Governance. Role: Sets direction and checks results. Example: The board approves the security strategy and policy. Management. Role: Plans and runs the work. Example: The security manager runs the program. Operations. Role: Does the daily tasks. Example: An analyst applies a procedure. Exam tip: Governance equals direction and oversight. Management equals execution. Senior management owns policy and accepts risk.

1.title: Regulations and laws
1.text: Regulations and laws. Laws and regulations are mandatory and come from governments or regulators. Breaking them can bring fines, lawsuits or prison and harms reputation. Compliance means following them. G D P R (E U). Privacy of personal data of people in the E U. hip ah (U S). Health information. S O X (U S). Financial reporting accuracy of public companies. G L B A (U S). Financial institutions and customer data. F E R P A (U S). Student education records. C C P A (California). Consumer privacy.

1.title: Regulations and laws, continued
1.text: Regulations and laws. P C I D S S (payment card security) is not a law: it is an industry standard that card brands require by contract. Exam tip: A law is mandatory by government. A standard like P C I D S S is mandatory by contract. When laws from several places apply, the strictest applicable one often drives the design.

1.title: Frameworks and guidelines
1.text: Frameworks and guidelines. A framework is a structured set of good practices to organize a security program. It is voluntary unless a law or contract requires it.

1.title: Frameworks and guidelines, continued
1.text: Frameworks and guidelines. The figure shows this: Frameworks guide the program; policy, standards, procedures and guidelines apply it.

1.title: Frameworks and guidelines, continued
1.text: Frameworks and guidelines. nist Cybersecurity Framework (C S F). Functions Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. nist S P eight hundred fifty-three. A catalog of security and privacy controls. I S O I E C twenty-seven thousand one. Requirements for an information security management system (I S M S); organizations can be audited against it. I S O I E C twenty-seven thousand two. Guidance on the controls. C I S Controls. A prioritized list of practical safeguards from the Center for Internet Security. C O B I T. A framework for I T governance and management.

1.title: Policies, standards, procedures and guidelines
1.text: Policies, standards, procedures and guidelines. Policy. Purpose: High-level rule that states what and why; approved by senior management. Mandatory?: Yes. Example: "All laptops must be encrypted". Standard. Purpose: Specific requirements that support a policy. Mandatory?: Yes. Example: "Use A E S with a two hundred fifty-six-bit key". Procedure. Purpose: Step-by-step instructions for a task. Mandatory?: Yes. Example: "How to enable disk encryption". Guideline. Purpose: Recommendations and advice. Mandatory?: No. Example: "Prefer a passphrase of several words". A baseline is the minimum secure configuration for a type of system. Common policies: acceptable use, password, remote access, data classification, data retention, incident response, bring your own device (B Y O D). Exam tip: Policy says what and why. Standard says which. Procedure says how. Guideline is only advice. The order: policy first, then standards, then procedures.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Which document gives step-by-step instructions for restoring a database from backup? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A procedure, which lists the steps to follow. A procedure is a set of step-by-step instructions for a task.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A document says that passwords must have at least fourteen characters. Which type of document is it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: A standard, which states a specific requirement. A specific, mandatory requirement that supports a policy is a standard.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A company stores payment card data and must follow P C I D S S. How is P C I D S S best described? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: An industry standard required by contract. P C I D S S is an industry standard that card brands require by contract; it is not a law.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A team wants to build a security program using the functions Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, plus Govern. Which framework is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: The nist Cybersecurity Framework. The nist Cybersecurity Framework is organized around those functions, including Govern.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Who is responsible for approving the security policy of an organization? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Senior management or the board. Policy is approved by senior management, which sets direction and owns the risk.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A recommendation that staff should use a long passphrase, but it is not required, is an example of what? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: A guideline, which is optional. A guideline is a recommendation and is not mandatory.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Which document is mandatory and high level? Answer: A policy. Question two. Which document is optional advice? Answer: A guideline. Question three. What does I S O I E C twenty-seven thousand one define? Answer: Requirements for an information security management system.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Is P C I D S S a law? Answer: No, it is an industry standard required by contract. Question five. What are the nist C S F (critical success factor) functions? Answer: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. Question six. Who approves policy? Answer: Senior management.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Governance: leaders direct and oversee; management executes. Laws: mandatory by government: G D P R, hip ah, S O X. P C I D S S: industry standard, mandatory by contract. Frameworks: nist C S F, nist eight hundred fifty-three, I S O twenty-seven thousand one and twenty-seven thousand two, C I S Controls, C O B I T. Documents: policy (what, why), standard (which), procedure (how), guideline (advice).
